name: Stovepipe and chimney pipe
summary: Pipe that carries wood-stove smoke outside: single-wall and double-wall stovepipe inside the room, and insulated factory-built chimney through walls, ceilings and roofs.
uses: Single-wall black stovepipe, 24 gauge or heavier: connects the stove to the chimney in the open room only, at least 450 mm (18 in) from anything that burns (NRCan wood heating)
Double-wall stovepipe: the same job with about 150 mm (6 in) clearance; still a connector only, never through a wall or ceiling (Woodstock close clearance)

Insulated 650 °C factory-built chimney (ULC S629, UL 103HT): the pipe made to go through a wall, ceiling or roof, with its own thimble and supports and the maker's clearance (2 in, 50 mm, for DuraTech) (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent DTC)

Not for wood stoves: galvanised pipe or duct (the coating vaporises into dangerous gas), B-vent (listed gas appliances only) and pellet vent (for pellet stoves, which don't need a high-temperature chimney) (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent B-vent)
Spare black pipe and elbows: outdoor builds such as a rocket stove's chimney. Never galvanised near the fire (NRCan wood heating)
identify: Single-wall stovepipe is plain black-painted steel, one layer, with a crimped (male) end and a plain end; it comes in 150, 175 and 200 mm (6, 7 and 8 in) and must be at least 24 gauge (NRCan wood heating). Double-wall stovepipe has a stainless inner pipe, an air gap and a steel outer casing (aluminised on Selkirk DSP), and on Selkirk DSP the visible crimp is on the female end (Woodstock close clearance). Insulated chimney, often sold as Class A (Cornell wood stove safety), is a thick stainless tube, about 200 mm (8 in) outside for a 150 mm (6 in) flue, with insulation between the walls (NRCan wood heating, DuraVent DTC); its label gives ULC S629 in Canada or UL 103HT in the US and a 650 °C (1,200 °F) rating (DuraVent DTC). A thinner chimney with 25 mm (1 in) walls is made for some factory-built fireplaces, not stoves, and the old Type A chimney (built for oil furnaces; NRCan says it was used before 1983, CMHC before 1981) is not suitable for wood either (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). B-vent has a galvanised steel outer pipe and an aluminium inner pipe, marked UL 441 or CAN/ULC-S605 (DuraVent B-vent). Pellet vent is a light double-wall pipe for pellet stoves, which don't need a high-temperature chimney; a wood stove does (NRCan wood heating).
test: Read the label on any double-wall or insulated pipe: no listing, no use through a wall. Squeeze single-wall pipe that has been in use: the walls should not crush (Cornell wood stove safety). Look for rust, pinholes, corrosion at the joints and bulges in a chimney's inner liner (NRCan wood heating). Pipe that has glowed red has been overfired, which can damage it for good (DuraVent DTC). After a chimney fire, metal chimney is checked for separated joints, warping, buckling and open seams, and the damage is often out of sight (CSIA after-fire). Use only parts made for that brand and model of insulated chimney (Drolet Part 1).

decay.note: New pipe kept dry lasts for years. Pipe in service corrodes from creosote and summer damp, and a chimney fire can warp it.

improvise: Nothing improvised goes through a wall, ceiling, roof, tent or earth wall: single-wall and double-wall stovepipe are connectors only (Woodstock close clearance, Drolet Part 1), and only a listed solid-fuel chimney or a lined masonry chimney takes a wood stove (Drolet Part 1). Furnace and water-heater B-vent is for gas only (DuraVent B-vent). Galvanised pipe and duct give off dangerous gas when hot, and dryer duct is not stovepipe: connector pipe must be at least 24-gauge steel (NRCan wood heating), and Drolet warns against makeshift materials (Drolet Part 1). Short of pipe, keep the run short and straight and go up rather than sideways; a window is not a way out for the pipe: the stove install guide says why.
